title: SPARK CSEC Physics - Paper 02 Practice Paper 1
subject: Physics
syllabus: CXC 22/G/SYLL 13, for examinations from May and June 2015
instructions: This paper consists of SIX questions in TWO sections. Answer ALL questions.
Write your answers in the spaces provided in this booklet.
Do NOT write in the margins.
Where appropriate, ALL WORKING MUST BE SHOWN in this booklet.
You may use a silent, non-programmable calculator. Note that an answer given to an inappropriate number of figures will be penalised.
required_materials: Graph paper or an on-screen grid

mark_scheme_key.M: Method mark. Awarded for the right approach and a correct substitution, whether or not the arithmetic that follows is right.
mark_scheme_key.A: Accuracy mark. Awarded for the correct value, with its unit, to the precision asked for. Normally depends on the method mark before it.
mark_scheme_key.B: Independent mark. Stands on its own and depends on nothing earlier: a definition, a named source of error, a labelled axis.

marking_conventions: A correct final answer implies the method, unless the question demanded the working.
Follow through. Where a candidate uses their own wrong value correctly in a later part, mark that later part on their value.
A missing unit is penalised once per question, not once per part.
An answer given to more figures than asked for keeps the mark. An answer with fewer figures than the data justify loses it.

marking_coverage.note: A criterion carrying a `check` is marked automatically. A criterion carrying `manual: true` is for prose, a drawn graph or a completed table, which cannot be judged from a typed string without a keyword list written for that answer. The engine reports a manual criterion as something to check against the worked solution rather than counting it as lost.

provenance: Original questions written for SPARK. The structure, language, mark allocations and question archetypes follow the CSEC Physics Paper 02 papers of 2008 to 2023. No past-paper question is reproduced. This is not a Caribbean Examinations Council publication.

questions.paper: SPARK CSEC Physics Practice Paper 02 number 1
questions.stem: A student investigated how the pressure of a fixed mass of gas depends on its volume. The temperature of the gas was kept constant throughout the experiment. The volume, V, of the gas and the pressure, P, of the gas were recorded in Table 1.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Complete Table 1 by calculating the missing values.
parts.solution:
1/V for 12.0 cm³ = 8.33 × 10⁻²; for 20.0 cm³ = 5.00 × 10⁻²; for 30.0 cm³ = 3.33 × 10⁻²

Marker's note. Accept 8.3, 5.0 and 3.3. Do not penalise a candidate who works in cm⁻³ without the × 10⁻² so long as the values are consistent with the column heading.
parts.markerNote: Accept 8.3, 5.0 and 3.3. Do not penalise a candidate who works in cm⁻³ without the × 10⁻² so long as the values are consistent with the column heading.

criteria.description: divides 1 by the volume for at least one row

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: On the grid provided on page 4, plot a graph of pressure, P/kPa, against 1/V (cm⁻³) × 10⁻², using 2 cm to represent 1 × 10⁻² cm⁻³ on the horizontal axis and 2 cm to represent 40 kPa on the vertical axis.
parts.answer: A straight line through the origin
parts.solution:
A straight line through the origin

Marker's note. A dot to dot line scores nothing for B4. A line drawn with a ruler which misses the origin still scores B4 if the points justify it.
parts.markerNote: A dot to dot line scores nothing for B4. A line drawn with a ruler which misses the origin still scores B4 if the points justify it.

criteria.description: both axes labelled with the quantity and its unit
the scales asked for are used, and the points fill at least half the grid
all six points plotted correctly; deduct one mark for each point misplaced
a single best fit straight line drawn through the points and the origin

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Determine the gradient of the graph, stating its unit.
parts.answer: gradient = 2400 kPa cm³
parts.solution:
gradient = 2400 kPa cm³

Marker's note. The gradient is P ÷ (1/V), so the unit is kPa ÷ cm⁻³, which is kPa cm³. Accept the unit written as kPa cm³ or as kPa/cm⁻³. A gradient taken from two table values instead of from the line loses M1 but may still earn A1.
parts.markerNote: The gradient is P ÷ (1/V), so the unit is kPa ÷ cm⁻³, which is kPa cm³. Accept the unit written as kPa cm³ or as kPa/cm⁻³. A gradient taken from two table values instead of from the line loses M1 but may still earn A1.

criteria.description: a triangle drawn on the line, using at least half its length

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Use the graph to determine the pressure of the gas when its volume is 18.0 cm³.
parts.answer: 133 kPa
parts.solution:
133 kPa

Marker's note. A candidate who calculates 2400/18 rather than reading the graph has not done what was asked but has the physics right: award M1 and A1, withhold M2. Follow through from the candidate's own earlier value.
parts.markerNote: A candidate who calculates 2400/18 rather than reading the graph has not done what was asked but has the physics right: award M1 and A1, withhold M2. Follow through from the candidate's own earlier value.

criteria.description: reads the pressure off the line at that value of 1/V

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Complete the following statement.
parts.answer: inversely proportional; temperature; the constant PV for that mass of gas
parts.solution:
inversely proportional; temperature; the constant PV for that mass of gas

Marker's note. For B3 accept 'the constant in PV = constant', or 'P × V', or the numerical value 2400 kPa cm³.
parts.markerNote: For B3 accept 'the constant in PV = constant', or 'P × V', or the numerical value 2400 kPa cm³.

criteria.description: the product of pressure and volume, PV, for that mass of gas

blanks: Boyle's law states that the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is ...............................
to its volume, provided the ............................... of the gas is kept constant.
The gradient of the graph in Figure 1 is equal to ............................... .

parts.label: (f)
parts.prompt: State ONE precaution that the student should have taken while carrying out this experiment.
parts.answer: Allow time for the temperature of the gas to settle before each reading is taken
parts.solution:
Allow time for the temperature of the gas to settle before each reading is taken

Marker's note. Accept: wait for the temperature to become steady, since the law holds only at constant temperature; read the scale square on to avoid parallax; check the gauge for a zero error; change the volume slowly so that no heating occurs. Award one mark only where the precaution is named without a reason. Refuse 'be careful' and 'avoid human error'.

questions.paper: SPARK CSEC Physics Practice Paper 02 number 1

parts.label: (a) (i)
parts.prompt: Define the term 'density'.
parts.answer: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance.
parts.solution:
Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance.

Marker's note. Accept density = mass ÷ volume.
parts.markerNote: Accept density = mass ÷ volume.

parts.prompt: State the SI unit of density.
parts.answer: kg m⁻³
parts.solution:
kg m⁻³

parts.markerNote: Accept kg/m³. Do not accept g cm⁻³, which is not the SI unit.

parts.prompt:
A solid rectangular block has sides of length 20 cm, 10 cm and 5.0 cm. The mass of the block is 2.7 kg.

Calculate the volume of the block, in m³.
parts.solution:
1.0 × 10⁻³ m³

Marker's note. 0.20 × 0.10 × 0.050. A candidate who works in cm³ and gets 1000 cm³ earns M1 only, unless the conversion to m³ then follows.
parts.markerNote: 0.20 × 0.10 × 0.050. A candidate who works in cm³ and gets 1000 cm³ earns M1 only, unless the conversion to m³ then follows.

2700 kg m⁻³

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Define the term 'pressure' and state the formula used to calculate it.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The block is placed on a bench so that it rests on its largest face. Calculate the pressure exerted by the block on the bench. [Take g as 10 N kg⁻¹.]
parts.solution:
1350 Pa

Marker's note. Accept 1.35 × 10³ Pa or 1350 N m⁻². A candidate who uses the mass in place of the weight and gets 135 loses A1 but keeps M2.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: State, giving a reason, which face of the block would exert the greatest pressure on the bench.
parts.answer: The smallest face, because pressure is inversely proportional to area for a fixed force.

The smallest face, because pressure is inversely proportional to area for a fixed force.

parts.label: (f)
parts.prompt: A diver descends to a depth of 15 m below the surface of the sea. Calculate the pressure on the diver due to the sea water alone. [Density of sea water = 1030 kg m⁻³.]
parts.solution:
1.55 × 10⁵ Pa

Marker's note. The question asks for the pressure due to the water alone, so atmospheric pressure is not to be added. A candidate who adds 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa has answered a different question and loses A1 but keeps M1.

questions.paper: SPARK CSEC Physics Practice Paper 02 number 1

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the principle of conservation of energy.
parts.answer: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form to another.
parts.solution:
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form to another.

Marker's note. Accept 'the total energy of a closed system is constant' for both marks.
parts.markerNote: Accept 'the total energy of a closed system is constant' for both marks.

criteria.description: energy cannot be created or destroyed
it is converted from one form to another, or transferred from one body to another

parts.label: (b) (i)
parts.prompt:
An electric pump raises 500 kg of water from a well through a vertical height of 12 m in 40 s. [Take g as 10 N kg⁻¹.]

Calculate the work done by the pump against gravity.
parts.solution:
6.0 × 10⁴ J

Marker's note. Accept 6.0 × 10⁴ J or 60 kJ.
parts.markerNote: Accept 6.0 × 10⁴ J or 60 kJ.

parts.label: (b) (ii)
parts.prompt:
An electric pump raises 500 kg of water from a well through a vertical height of 12 m in 40 s. [Take g as 10 N kg⁻¹.]

Calculate the useful power output of the pump.
parts.solution:
1500 W

Marker's note. Follow through from the candidate's own earlier value. Accept 1.5 kW.
parts.markerNote: Follow through from the candidate's own earlier value. Accept 1.5 kW.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The pump draws 2500 W of electrical power from the supply. Calculate the efficiency of the pump.
parts.answer: 60 per cent
parts.solution:
60 per cent

Marker's note. Follow through from the candidate's own earlier value. A candidate who leaves the answer as 0.6 without the percentage earns M1 and A1 but not M2.

Some of the input energy is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy, through friction in the moving parts and resistance in the wires.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: State TWO renewable sources of energy which are suitable for generating electricity on a Caribbean island, and state ONE advantage of using them instead of imported fuel.
parts.answer: Solar and wind. The fuel is free and does not have to be imported, which saves foreign exchange.
parts.solution:
Solar and wind. The fuel is free and does not have to be imported, which saves foreign exchange.

Marker's note. Accept solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass and wave. Do not accept natural gas or nuclear, which are not renewable. For B3 accept: no fuel to import, saves foreign exchange, no carbon dioxide produced during generation, the supply cannot be cut off by a shipping problem.
parts.markerNote: Accept solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass and wave. Do not accept natural gas or nuclear, which are not renewable. questions.paper: SPARK CSEC Physics Practice Paper 02 number 1

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Distinguish between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave, and give ONE example of EACH.
parts.answer: In a transverse wave the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel; in a longitudinal wave they vibrate along it. Examples: light or a water wave; sound.
parts.solution:
In a transverse wave the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel; in a longitudinal wave they vibrate along it. Examples: light or a water wave; sound.

Marker's note. The distinction must be made on the direction of vibration relative to the direction of travel. 'One goes up and down and the other goes along' scores nothing, since both travel along. Accept any electromagnetic wave, or a wave on a rope or water, for B3. B4 requires sound, or a compression wave in a spring.
parts.markerNote: The distinction must be made on the direction of vibration relative to the direction of travel. 'One goes up and down and the other goes along' scores nothing, since both travel along. Accept any electromagnetic wave, or a wave on a rope or water, for B3. B4 requires sound, or a compression wave in a spring.

criteria.description: transverse: vibration at right angles to the direction of travel
longitudinal: vibration along the direction of travel
a correct example of a transverse wave
a correct example of a longitudinal wave

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A wave travelling through air has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.66 m. Calculate the speed of the wave.
parts.answer: 330 m s⁻¹
parts.solution: 330 m s⁻¹

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A boy standing 165 m from a vertical cliff claps his hands once and hears the echo 1.0 s later. Calculate the speed of sound in air, as measured by the boy.
parts.answer: 330 m s⁻¹
parts.solution:
330 m s⁻¹

Marker's note. Forgetting to double the distance gives 165 m s⁻¹: award M2 only. This is the commonest error in the question.
parts.markerNote: Forgetting to double the distance gives 165 m s⁻¹: award M2 only. This is the commonest error in the question.

criteria.description: recognises that the sound travels 2 × 165 = 330 m

parts.label: (d) (i)
parts.prompt: State what is meant by the term 'ultrasound'.
parts.answer: Sound of a frequency above the upper limit of human hearing, above about 20 kHz.
parts.solution:
Sound of a frequency above the upper limit of human hearing, above about 20 kHz.

Marker's note. Accept 'above 20 000 Hz'.
parts.markerNote: Accept 'above 20 000 Hz'.

criteria.description: frequency above the range of human hearing

parts.label: (d) (ii)
parts.prompt: State ONE use of ultrasound and explain why ultrasound is suitable for that use.
parts.answer: Scanning an unborn baby. Ultrasound is not ionising, so it does not damage living cells.
parts.solution:
Scanning an unborn baby. Ultrasound is not ionising, so it does not damage living cells.

Marker's note. Accept: pre-natal scanning, imaging soft tissue, breaking up kidney stones, depth sounding at sea, checking castings for cracks. The reason must fit the use: for a medical use, that ultrasound does not ionise and so does not damage cells; for depth sounding, that sound travels well through water while light does not.
parts.markerNote: Accept: pre-natal scanning, imaging soft tissue, breaking up kidney stones, depth sounding at sea, checking castings for cracks. criteria.description: a reason connected to that use

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: State the wave parameter which determines EACH of the following.
parts.answer: Pitch is determined by frequency. Loudness is determined by amplitude.
parts.solution:
Pitch is determined by frequency. Loudness is determined by amplitude.

Marker's note. Do not accept wavelength for pitch, since the question asks for the wave parameter which determines it and the medium fixes the relationship.
parts.markerNote: Do not accept wavelength for pitch, since the question asks for the wave parameter which determines it and the medium fixes the relationship.

questions.paper: SPARK CSEC Physics Practice Paper 02 number 1

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Define the term 'half-life' of a radioactive source.
parts.answer: The half-life is the time taken for half the nuclei of a radioactive sample to decay, or for the activity to fall to half its original value.
parts.solution:
The half-life is the time taken for half the nuclei of a radioactive sample to decay, or for the activity to fall to half its original value.

Marker's note. Accept either the nuclei form or the activity form. 'The time for the source to decay' scores nothing.
parts.markerNote: Accept either the nuclei form or the activity form. 'The time for the source to decay' scores nothing.

criteria.description: for half the undecayed nuclei to decay, or for the activity to halve

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Complete Table 2 for the three types of emission from radioactive sources.
parts.answer: Alpha: helium nucleus, +2, stopped by paper. Beta: fast-moving electron, −1, stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Gamma: electromagnetic radiation, 0, reduced by several centimetres of lead.
parts.solution:
Alpha: helium nucleus, +2, stopped by paper. Beta: fast-moving electron, −1, stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Gamma: electromagnetic radiation, 0, reduced by several centimetres of lead.

Marker's note. For gamma, accept 'reduced by lead' rather than 'stopped by lead'; gamma is never completely stopped, so do not require the word stopped. A candidate who writes 'electron' for beta without 'fast moving' or 'from the nucleus' still earns the charge and penetration marks.
parts.markerNote: For gamma, accept 'reduced by lead' rather than 'stopped by lead'; gamma is never completely stopped, so do not require the word stopped. A candidate who writes 'electron' for beta without 'fast moving' or 'from the nucleus' still earns the charge and penetration marks.

criteria.description: alpha is a helium nucleus, or 2 protons and 2 neutrons
alpha is stopped by paper, or by a few centimetres of air
beta has a relative charge of −1
beta is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium
gamma is electromagnetic radiation, or a high energy photon

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The count rate from a radioactive source, corrected for background radiation, falls from 800 counts per minute to 50 counts per minute in 60 minutes. Determine the half-life of the source.
parts.answer: 15 minutes
parts.solution:
15 minutes

Marker's note. A candidate who divides 60 by 2 and answers 30 minutes has counted one halving rather than four: award M1 only. Working shown as a table or a sketch graph is acceptable for M1 and M2.
parts.markerNote: A candidate who divides 60 by 2 and answers 30 minutes has counted one halving rather than four: award M1 only. Working shown as a table or a sketch graph is acceptable for M1 and M2.

criteria.description: identifies that four half-lives have passed

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: State ONE beneficial use of a radioactive isotope, and TWO precautions which should be taken when handling radioactive sources.
parts.answer: Use: tracing a leak in an underground pipe. Precautions: handle the source with tongs, and store it in a lead-lined container.
parts.solution:
Use: tracing a leak in an underground pipe. Precautions: handle the source with tongs, and store it in a lead-lined container.

Marker's note. Uses: medical tracers, treating cancer, sterilising equipment, dating rocks or archaeological remains, thickness gauging, detecting leaks, smoke alarms. Precautions: handle with tongs or forceps, never with bare hands; keep the source pointed away from the body; store in a lead-lined container; limit the time of exposure; wear a film badge. 'Be careful' scores nothing.
